source_text: Ibi namque hic est a me collatus ordo verborum, cum dixissem auctorem Deum caeli et terrae, omniumque quae in eis sunt, ac per hoc et hominum propter quos cuncta facta sunt. Non autem me fugit - inquio - cum haec dicimus, illud de nobis disseminandum esse, quia gratiam Christi necessariam parvulis non putemus. Quod christianos populos laudabiliter et vehementer offendit; si tamen dicti per se nefarii non nos arbitrarentur auctores; eo enim modo nec de fratribus suis falsa credendo crimen incurrerent, et studiosos se circa amorem fidei comprobarent. Munienda igitur nobis ista pars est contra impetum vanitatis, et confessione brevi os obloquentium consuendum. Nos igitur in tantum gratiam Baptismatis omnibus utilem aetatibus confitemur, ut cunctos, qui illam non necessariam etiam parvulis putant, aeterno feriamus anathemate. Sed hanc gratiam locupletem spiritalibus donis credimus, quae multis opima muneribus ac reverenda virtutibus, pro infirmitatum generibus et humanorum statuum diversitatibus, una, tam remediorum collatrice quam munerum, virtute medicatur. Quae cum admovetur, non est mutanda pro causis; iam enim ipsa dona sua pro accedentium capacitate dispensat. Sicut enim artes omnes non pro diversitate materiarum, quas arripiunt excolendas, ipsae quoque aut detrimenta aut augmenta patiuntur, sed idem semper atque uno modo se habentes multiplici decorantur effectu; ita et secundum Apostolum: "a fides, unum Baptisma " [n95] . Et multiplicantur et dilatantur in donis, nec tamen in mysteriorum mutantur ordinibus. Sed haec gratia non adversatur iustitiae, quae maculas eluit iniquitatis; nec facit peccata, sed purgat; quae absolvit reos, non calumniatur innocuos. Christus enim, qui est sui operis redemptor, auget circa imaginem suam continua largitate beneficia; et quos fecerat condendo bonos, facit innovando adoptandoque meliores [n96] . Hanc igitur gratiam, per quam reis venia, illuminatio spiritalis, adoptio filiorum Dei, municipatus Hierusalem caelestis, sanctificatio atque in Christi membra translatio, et possessio Regni caelorum mortalibus datur, qui aliquibus negandam putat, omnium bonorum exsecrationem meretur.
pass_a_gloss: For there this order of words was brought together by me, when I had said that God is author of heaven and of earth, and of all things which are in them, and through this also of humans for whose sake all things were made. But it does not escape me — I say — when we say these things, that that is to be disseminated about us, that we do not think the grace of Christ necessary for little ones. Which laudably and vehemently offends Christian peoples; if only they did not think us authors of a saying wicked through itself; for in that way they would neither incur a charge by believing false things about their own brothers, and they would prove themselves studious about the love of the faith. This part therefore must be fortified by us against the attack of vanity, and the mouth of those speaking against must be sewn with a brief confession. We therefore confess the grace of Baptism useful to all ages to such a point, that we strike with eternal anathema all who think it not necessary even for little ones. But we believe this grace rich with spiritual gifts, which, fat with many munera and to be revered with virtues, according to the kinds of infirmities and the diversities of human states, heals by one virtue, as much a bringer-together of remedies as of gifts. Which when it is applied, is not to be changed according to cases; for already it dispenses its own gifts according to the capacity of those approaching. For as all arts, not according to the diversity of materials which they snatch up to be cultivated, themselves also suffer either losses or increases, but always the same and holding themselves in one manner are adorned by a multiple effect; so also according to the Apostle: one faith, one Baptism. Both they are multiplied and they are widened in gifts, nor nevertheless are they changed in the orders of the mysteries. But this grace is not adverse to justice, which washes the stains of iniquity; nor does it make sins, but purges; which absolves the guilty, does not slander the harmless. For Christ, who is redeemer of his own work, increases benefits around his image by continual largesse; and those whom he had made good by founding, he makes better by renewing and adopting. This grace therefore, through which pardon for the guilty, spiritual illumination, adoption of sons of God, citizenship of the heavenly Jerusalem, sanctification and translation into the members of Christ, and possession of the Kingdom of the heavens is given to mortals, whoever thinks it to be denied to some, deserves the execration of all good people.

pass_b_english: For there I set out the following sequence of words, after saying that God is the author of heaven and earth and everything in them, and therefore also of human beings, for whose sake all things were made (compare Genesis 1:1; Exodus 20:11). I said: “I am aware that when we say these things, a report will be spread about us that we do not think Christ's grace necessary for infants. Such a statement rightly and deeply offends Christian people. If only they did not suppose us responsible for a saying that is wicked in itself! Then they would not incur guilt by believing falsehoods about their brothers, and they would show their devotion to the love of the faith. We must therefore defend this position against the assault of empty talk and sew up the mouths of our detractors with a brief confession.

We acknowledge that the grace of baptism is beneficial to every age, so completely that we pronounce an eternal anathema on all who think it unnecessary even for infants. But we believe this grace to be rich in spiritual gifts. Abundant in its many favors and worthy of reverence for its powers, it heals the different kinds of weakness and the different conditions of human beings by one power that bestows both remedies and gifts. When it is administered, it does not need to be changed to suit particular cases: it distributes its own gifts according to the capacity of those who approach. No craft itself suffers loss or gain because of the different materials it takes up to work on; remaining always the same and in the same condition, it is adorned by a variety of effects. In the same way, according to the apostle, there is ‘one faith, one baptism’ (Ephesians 4:5). These multiply and expand in their gifts, yet are not changed in the order of their mysteries.

But this grace, which washes away the stains of injustice, does not oppose justice. It does not create sins but cleanses them; it acquits the guilty, not falsely accuses the innocent. Christ, the redeemer of his own work, increases his benefits toward his image with continual generosity. Those whom he made good by creating them he makes better by renewing and adopting them” (quoted also in Augustine, Against Julian 3.8 and following). Through this grace, pardon for the guilty, spiritual illumination, adoption as God's children, citizenship in the heavenly Jerusalem, sanctification, incorporation into Christ's members, and possession of the kingdom of heaven are given to mortals. Anyone who thinks this grace should be denied to anyone deserves the abhorrence of all good people (compare Ephesians 1:5; Ephesians 2:19; Hebrews 12:22–23; 1 Corinthians 12:13).
